questions.q: A checkout Pod has been stuck in `Pending` for ten minutes. What is the correct next step to find out why?
options: kubectl logs the Pod — Pending Pods always have useful logs
kubectl describe pod the Pod and read the Events section
Delete the Pod immediately and let the Deployment recreate it
Restart the entire cluster
questions.explain: A Pending Pod hasn't been scheduled yet, so it has no container logs. kubectl describe pod's Events section shows exactly what the scheduler tried and why it couldn't place the Pod (e.g. insufficient resources, an unsatisfied nodeSelector or taint).

questions.q: A Pod shows `CrashLoopBackOff`. What does that specific status mean, as opposed to `ImagePullBackOff`?
options: The image cannot be downloaded from the registry
The container successfully starts but then exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with increasing delay between attempts
The node the Pod is on is out of memory
The Pod has not been scheduled to any node yet
questions.explain: CrashLoopBackOff means the container does start — the image pulled fine — but it exits (crashes or completes) repeatedly, so Kubernetes keeps retrying with exponential backoff. ImagePullBackOff is specifically about the image never successfully pulling in the first place.

questions.q: A container just restarted after being OOMKilled. Which command shows the logs from the failed attempt, not the fresh restart?
options: kubectl logs <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl describe pod <pod> --logs
kubectl top pod <pod>
questions.explain: kubectl logs without a flag shows the current (restarted) container's logs, which won't contain the crash. --previous retrieves the logs from the prior, terminated instance of the container — where the actual failure was logged.

questions.q: Before patching and rebooting node-03 for maintenance, what is the correct sequence to avoid disrupting running workloads?
options: kubectl delete node node-03, then recreate it after maintenance
kubectl cordon node-03 to stop new scheduling, then kubectl drain node-03 --ignore-daemonsets to evict existing Pods elsewhere, then patch/reboot, then kubectl uncordon node-03
Just reboot the node directly — Kubernetes handles everything automatically with no preparation needed
kubectl taint node-03 maintenance=true, which immediately removes all Pods with no further action needed
questions.explain: Cordon prevents new Pods from landing on the node being serviced; drain safely evicts the Pods already there so they reschedule elsewhere; only then is the node safe to take offline. Uncordon returns it to the scheduling pool once maintenance is done.

questions.q: Why does `kubectl drain` require the `--ignore-daemonsets` flag to succeed on a node running DaemonSet Pods?
options: Because DaemonSet Pods cannot be evicted from a node at all; the flag tells drain to skip them rather than fail
Because DaemonSets always run with root privileges
Because --ignore-daemonsets deletes the DaemonSet resource entirely
Because drain cannot run on any node that has a DaemonSet in the cluster
questions.explain: DaemonSet Pods are designed to run one copy per node as a matter of their controller's logic, so a normal drain can't meaningfully evict and reschedule them elsewhere. --ignore-daemonsets tells drain to proceed and leave those specific Pods alone rather than error out.
